You report what someone else said in the past: you change the tenses (vengo → venía, vendré → vendría), the questions (me preguntó si…, me preguntó dónde…) and the orders (me pidió que + imperfect subjunctive).
Kenji told me he would come in December.
She asked me if I was tired.
I asked him where he lived.
He asked me to wait for him.
She said she had already bought the tickets.
To change the tenses in reported speech when the reporting verb is in the past.
To change expressions of time and place (mañana → al día siguiente, aquí → allí).
To report questions: preguntó si… / preguntó qué, dónde, cuándo…
To report orders and requests: me pidió / me dijo que + imperfect subjunctive.
To use more precise communication verbs than “decir”.
December, Bucharest. Mihai comes home from the hospital. Ana has spent all day on the phone with friends in Madrid and has to tell him everything.
How was your day? Did you talk to anyone?
To the whole of Madrid. First Kenji called. He told me he’d bought the tickets and that he’s coming with Haruka and Sakura on the twentieth of January.
The twentieth? But the baby’s due around the fifteenth.
That’s what I told him. He answered that that’s exactly why: he wanted to arrive when we were already home, so as not to be in the way.
Typical Kenji. And who else called?
Yuki, from Tokyo. She asked me if I was scared of giving birth. I told her a little, but that you’re a doctor.
A cardiologist, Ana. Not a gynaecologist.
That’s what she told me too, laughing. And she asked me what name we were going to give her in the end. I explained that it’s still Rosa Elena.
And your mother? I’m sure she called too.
Three times. The first time, she asked me to eat more. The second time, she asked if we’d bought the pram. The third time, she told me not to worry about anything.
She sent me a voice message. She said the club had made a present for the baby and that she’d send it next week. She added that Tama had slept on it for a whole day.
So the present will arrive covered in cat hair.
Probably. Oh, and your mother called too. Well, she called Mrs Maria, and Mrs Maria came over to pass on the message.
I’m not sure. Mrs Maria explained it with gestures. I think she said your mother is coming tomorrow with a suitcase… or that she’s slaughtered a pig. One of the two.
“íbamos a poner” = we were going to give
“no me preocupara” = not to worry (imperf. subj.)
In reported speech, the voice is flatter, like a storyteller’s: «Me dijo que vendría…» No exclamations or questions in your voice.
ben-DREE-a, ten-DREE-a: stress on the í, and “dr” together. Not “vendiría”!
O-SEH-a: “I mean, so”. Spaniards use it constantly in conversation, sometimes several times per sentence.
When the reporting verb is in the PAST (dijo, explicó, contó), the tenses of what was said “move one step back”. You saw this rule at A2 (chapter 35). Now you complete it:
Dijo que venía al día siguiente. (imperfect)
Dijo que había comprado los billetes. (pluperfect)
Dijo que había comprado / compró los billetes.
English does the same: “I’m coming tomorrow” → “He said he WAS coming the next day”; “I will come” → “He said he WOULD come”. Trust your English instinct here!
If what was said is still true, you can keep the present: Me dijo que se llama Ilie (he’s still called that).
2. Changing words of time and place
This only happens if the moment has changed. If Ana is telling today what Kenji said today, she keeps “mañana”.
Me preguntó qué nombre le íbamos a poner.
The question word keeps its written accent: preguntó DÓNDE, QUÉ, CUÁNDO, CÓMO. The ¿? marks disappear.
For yes/no questions use “si” (if, whether), WITHOUT an accent. “Sí” with an accent means “yes”!
4. Orders and requests: que + imperfect subjunctive
When you report an order, advice or a request, the imperative becomes que + IMPERFECT SUBJUNCTIVE (the sequence of tenses from chapter 41):
Me dijo que no me preocupara.
Careful with “decir”: «Me dijo que venía» = he told me he WAS COMING (information). «Me dijo que viniera» = he told me TO COME (an order).
So you don’t keep repeating “dijo”, use verbs that show HOW something was said:
Me contó que se había casado.
Me explicó que no podía venir.
Añadió que Tama había dormido encima.
Me aseguró que todo saldría bien.
Se quejó de que nadie lo llamaba.
Useful expressions: por lo visto (apparently), según ella (according to her), al parecer (it seems).
“She asked me if I was all right.”
Me preguntó que si estoy bien.
He told me he would come with his family.
She asked me what name we were going to give her.
She asked me not to worry.
¿Qué le pidió Carmen la primera vez?
Que Tama había dormido encima del regalo
He promised me everything would be fine.
In the evening, Mihai calls his mother to find out what she actually meant to say. Then he tells Ana.
I’ve spoken to my mum. She told me she hadn’t slaughtered any pig. She says my uncle Petru did that, last week, for Christmas.
What she wanted to tell you was that she’s coming on the tenth of January, five days before the due date, and that she’ll stay a whole month.
She asked me if we had room for her. I told her yes, that she’d sleep in the room with the balcony.
She also asked us not to buy baby clothes, because she’s knitted “a few things”. When I asked her how much “a few things” was, she said just two suitcases.

She assured me she wouldn’t interfere in anything and that she was only coming to help. Then she added that, by the way, the baby would have to sleep with a red thread around her wrist, to ward off the evil eye.
I told her we’d discuss it. She answered that there was nothing to discuss. So now you know: red thread.
Que no compraran ropa de bebé
La noche del quince de enero
Later, when it was all over, everyone told the story of that night differently. But they all agreed on one thing: it all started with a soup.
Elena had been in Bucharest for five days. She had arrived on the tenth of January, as promised, with two suitcases of knitted clothes and a huge jar of frozen ciorbă “for emergencies”.

On the evening of the fifteenth, Elena heated up the ciorbă. Ana sat down at the table, tasted a spoonful and said it was delicious. Then she said her back was hurting a little. Then she said maybe it wasn’t her back.

According to Mihai, he stayed calm the whole time. According to Elena, her son put his shoes on the wrong feet, just like Kenji at his wedding, and spent ten minutes looking for the car keys while holding them in his hand.

According to Ana, Mihai asked her if she was all right about forty times on the way to the hospital. She answered yes the first twenty times. For the other twenty she asked him to be quiet and watch the road.
Mrs Maria, who saw everything from her window, told the whole neighbourhood the next day that the car had left “like a rocket” and had gone through two red lights. Mihai always denied it.

At the hospital, a very calm nurse explained that there were still a few hours to go. She asked Mihai to sit in the waiting room. Mihai told her he was a doctor. The nurse told him that tonight, he was the father.

Mihai sat down. Over the following hours he called everyone. He called Carmen, who told him she would catch the first plane in the morning. He called Grandma Rosario, who asked him every five minutes whether the baby had been born yet.
He called Kenji, who was asleep and who, according to Haruka, got out of bed, got dressed and packed his bag before remembering that his flight was in five days.
He called Grandpa Gheorghe. Grandpa listened in silence and told him just one thing: to remember to open the window of the room when the baby was born, to let in the air of the world.
At a quarter past five in the morning, the calm nurse came out into the waiting room. Mihai stood up so fast he knocked over a chair.
The nurse told him he could go in. She explained that the mother was fine, very tired, but fine. And she added, with a little smile, that the baby had excellent lungs.

Mihai went into the room. Ana was in bed, with her hair stuck to her forehead and her eyes shining. In her arms, wrapped in a white blanket, was a very small and very red being, crying with all her might.
“Let me introduce Rosa Elena,” said Ana. “She’s already made it clear she has opinions.”
Mihai had seen babies being born during his medical training. He had read books, he had studied. But nobody had warned him what he would feel at that moment.
Later, when people asked him what he had felt, he said it was as if the floor had disappeared and, at the same time, as if his feet were finally on solid ground.
He took his daughter in his arms. The baby suddenly stopped crying and looked at him, or so it seemed to him, with very serious dark eyes.
“Hola,” he said to her in Spanish. And then, in Romanian: “Bună, puiule.” (Hello, little one.)
Then he remembered what his grandfather had asked. He went to the window and opened it. Cold January air came in, smelling of snow and fresh bread from some nearby bakery.
The calm nurse came running in and asked him if he had gone mad, with the cold outside. Mihai explained that it was a family tradition. The nurse told him ten seconds, not one more.

It was ten seconds. But Mihai always said afterwards that it was enough. That Rosa Elena breathed the air of Bucharest for the first time, and it smelled of bread, like in the story of her great-grandfather Andrés.
When Elena arrived at the hospital at seven, she had a red thread in one hand and the jar of ciorbă in the other. She said it was for Ana, to get her strength back.
Ana looked at her and laughed for the first time in many hours. She asked Mihai to translate something for his mother. Mihai translated it.
She told her that next time she wanted to taste a soup, she would taste it very carefully.
Elena laughed so loudly that the calm nurse had to ask them, for the third time that morning, to keep their voices down.
That afternoon, when they were finally alone, Ana asked Mihai to tell her again what the nurse had said. Mihai told her. Ana closed her eyes and smiled.
“She was right,” she said. “Tonight you weren’t a doctor. You were the father. And you will be for the rest of your life.”

“ha dejado claro” = has made it clear
“se había vuelto loco” = had gone mad
“bajaran la voz” = keep their voices down (imperf. subj.)
